title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
summary: How matter exists as solids, liquids and gases, why tiny particles make each state behave differently, and how heating and cooling change one state into another.
poll: Heating and cooling are the most important ways to change matter.

versions.title: Solid, Liquid, Gas
versions.text:
Look at a rock. Look at a cup of tea. Feel the wind. All of them are matter. Matter is all the stuff in the world.

Most matter comes in three forms. It can be a solid. It can be a liquid. It can be a gas.

A rock is a solid. It keeps its shape. It does not flow. Ice is a solid, too.

Milk is a liquid. It can flow. Pour it in a cup. It takes the shape of the cup.

Air is a gas. You can not see it. A gas spreads out. It fills all the space it has.

Heat can change matter. Heat makes ice melt. The ice turns to water. Heat the water a lot. It turns to a gas.

Cold can change it back. Put a cold can in the sun. Drops form on it. The gas in the air turned back to water. Make water very cold. It turns to ice.

Big plants by the sea heat sea water. The water turns to a gas. The salt stays back. The gas cools. Now it is fresh water to drink.

versions.title: Solid, Liquid, Gas
versions.text:
Look at a rock, a glass of juice, and the air around you. They are all matter. Matter is the stuff that makes up the world.

Most matter comes in three forms. It can be a solid, a liquid, or a gas.

A rock is a solid. A solid keeps its own shape. Ice and wood are solids, too.

Juice is a liquid. A liquid can flow. When you pour it into a cup, it takes the shape of the cup.

Air is a gas. You can not see most gases. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it has.

All matter is made of tiny bits. They are too small to see. In a solid, the bits are packed close. In a gas, they are far apart and move fast.

Heat can change matter. When ice gets warm, it starts to melt. It turns into water. If you heat the water a lot, it boils. It turns into a gas.

Cold can change it back. On a hot day, drops form on a cold can. Gas in the air cooled and turned into water. Very cold water freezes into ice.

By the sea in Saudi Arabia, big plants heat sea water. The water turns into a gas, and the salt is left behind. The gas cools into fresh water to drink.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around you. You may see a stone, a glass of juice, and the steam from a hot drink. All of these things are matter. Matter is anything that takes up space.

Most matter on Earth comes in three forms. It can be a solid, a liquid, or a gas.

A stone is a solid. A solid has its own shape. If you put a stone in a box, it stays the same shape. Ice, wood, and metal are solids, too.

Juice is a liquid. A liquid can flow and pour. It takes the shape of the cup or bottle it is in. But it does not get bigger to fill the space.

Air is a gas. Most gases are clear, so you can not see them. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can find.

All matter is made of tiny bits called particles. They are much too small to see. In a solid, they are packed tight and only shake in place. In a liquid, they can slide past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and zoom around.

Heat can change matter from one form to another. When ice warms up, it starts to melt into water. If you heat water until it boils, it turns into a gas called water vapor.

Cooling can change matter back. On a hot day, drops form on a cold can. Water vapor in the air cooled and became liquid again. When water gets very cold, it freezes into ice.

On the coast of Saudi Arabia, big plants heat sea water. The water turns into a gas, but the salt stays behind. When the gas cools, it becomes fresh water for homes.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around your kitchen. You might see a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam rising from a pot of rice. These things look very different, but they are all matter. Matter is anything that takes up space and has weight.

Most matter on Earth is found in three forms, called states. It can be a solid, a liquid, or a gas.

A spoon is a solid. A solid has its own shape and size. If you move a spoon from a drawer to a bowl, its shape does not change. Ice, wood, and stone are solids, too.

Juice is a liquid. A liquid can flow and be poured. It takes the shape of whatever cup or bottle holds it. However, the amount of liquid stays the same.

Air is a gas. Most gases are invisible. A gas spreads out until it fills every corner of the space it is in.

All matter is made of tiny particles that are far too small to see. In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and only shake in place. In a liquid, they stay close but slide past each other. In a gas, they are spread far apart and move very fast.

Heating can change matter from one state to another. When ice warms up, it begins to melt into liquid water. When water is heated until it boils, it turns into a gas called water vapor.

Cooling can change matter back again. On a hot day, drops of water appear on a cold can. This happens because water vapor in the air cools down and becomes liquid. When liquid water gets cold enough, it freezes into solid ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, large plants heat seawater until it turns into a gas. The salt is left behind. When the gas cools, it becomes fresh water for millions of people.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around your kitchen. You might notice a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam rising from a pot of rice. These things seem very different from one another, yet they are all made of matter. Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.

Most matter on Earth exists in one of three forms, called states. These states are solid, liquid, and gas.

A spoon is a solid. A solid has a definite shape and size. Whether the spoon sits in a drawer or in a bowl, its shape does not change. Ice, wood, and stone are also solids.

Juice is a liquid. A liquid can flow and be poured, and it takes the shape of its container. However, the amount of liquid stays the same. A cup of juice poured into a tall bottle is still one cup of juice.

Air is a gas. Most gases are invisible, and a gas spreads out to fill any container completely, no matter how large it is.

The reason for these differences lies in particles, the tiny pieces that make up all matter. In a solid, particles are packed tightly together and can only vibrate in place. In a liquid, they stay close but can slide past one another. In a gas, they are far apart and move quickly in every direction.

Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster. When ice warms up, it begins to melt into liquid water. When water is heated enough, it boils and becomes a gas called water vapor. Water can also evaporate slowly at lower temperatures, which is why puddles dry up in the sun.

Cooling does the opposite. On a hot day, drops of water form on a cold can because water vapor in the air cools and turns back into liquid. This change is called condensation. When liquid water gets cold enough, it freezes into solid ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, large plants use these changes to make drinking water. They heat seawater until it turns into vapor, leaving the salt behind. Then they cool the vapor so it condenses into fresh water.

Cooling has the opposite effect. On a hot day, droplets form on a cold can because water vapor in the surrounding air cools and changes back into liquid. This process is called condensation. When liquid water becomes cold enough, it freezes into solid ice.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around your kitchen. You might notice a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam drifting upward from a pot of rice. These objects appear completely different from one another, yet they share an important feature: each of them is made of matter. Scientists define matter as anything that occupies space and has mass.

Most matter on Earth exists in one of three forms, which scientists call states. These states are solid, liquid, and gas.

A spoon is a solid. A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume, which means the amount of space it fills. Whether the spoon rests in a drawer or in a bowl of soup, its shape remains exactly the same. Ice, wood, and stone are also solids.

Juice is a liquid. A liquid flows and can be poured, and it takes the shape of whatever container holds it. However, its volume does not change. A cup of juice poured into a tall, narrow bottle is still precisely one cup of juice.

Air is a gas. Most gases are invisible, and a gas spreads out to fill any container completely, regardless of how large or unusually shaped the container may be.

The explanation for these differences lies in particles, the tiny pieces that make up all matter. In a solid, the particles are packed tightly together and can only vibrate in place. In a liquid, the particles remain close to one another but are able to slide past each other. In a gas, the particles are widely separated and travel rapidly in every direction.

Heating supplies particles with additional energy, so they move faster. When ice warms, it begins to melt into liquid water. When water is heated sufficiently, it boils and becomes a gas called water vapor. Water can also evaporate gradually at lower temperatures, which explains why puddles vanish on a sunny afternoon.

Cooling produces the opposite effect. On a hot day, droplets appear on a cold can because water vapor in the surrounding air cools and changes back into liquid. This process is called condensation. When liquid water becomes cold enough, it freezes into solid ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, enormous plants use these changes to produce drinking water. They heat seawater until it becomes vapor, leaving the salt behind, and then they cool the vapor so that it condenses into fresh water.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around your kitchen. You might notice a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam drifting upward from a pot of rice. These objects appear completely different from one another, yet they share an essential characteristic: each of them is composed of matter. Scientists define matter as anything that occupies space and possesses mass.

Most matter on Earth exists in one of three forms, which scientists refer to as states. These states are solid, liquid, and gas.

A spoon is a solid. A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume, meaning the amount of space it occupies. Whether the spoon rests in a drawer or in a bowl of soup, its shape remains identical. Ice, wood, and stone are additional examples of solids.

Juice is a liquid. A liquid flows and can be poured, and it adopts the shape of whatever container holds it. Nevertheless, its volume does not change; a cup of juice poured into a tall, narrow bottle is still precisely one cup of juice.

Air is a gas. Most gases are invisible, and a gas spreads out to fill any container entirely, regardless of how large or irregularly shaped that container may be.

The explanation for these differences involves particles, the microscopic pieces that make up all matter. In a solid, the particles are tightly packed and can only vibrate in fixed positions. In a liquid, the particles remain close to one another but are able to slide past each other. In a gas, the particles are widely separated and travel rapidly in every direction.

Heating supplies particles with additional energy, causing them to move faster. When ice warms, it begins to melt into liquid water. When water is heated sufficiently, it boils and transforms into a gas called water vapor. Water can also evaporate gradually at lower temperatures, which explains why puddles vanish on a sunny afternoon.

Cooling produces the opposite effect. On a hot day, droplets accumulate on a chilled can because water vapor in the surrounding air loses energy and changes back into liquid, a process called condensation. When liquid water becomes sufficiently cold, it freezes into solid ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, enormous facilities use these transformations to produce drinking water. They heat seawater until it becomes vapor, leaving the dissolved salt behind, and then they cool the vapor so that it condenses into fresh water for communities across the kingdom.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around your kitchen and you might notice a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam drifting upward from a pot of rice. These objects appear completely different from one another, yet they share an essential characteristic: each of them is composed of matter, which scientists define as anything that occupies space and possesses mass.

Most matter on Earth exists in one of three familiar forms, known as states: solid, liquid, and gas. Although the same substance can exist in all three states, each state behaves in its own distinctive way.

A spoon is a solid, which means it has a definite shape and a definite volume, or amount of space it occupies. Whether the spoon rests in a drawer or in a bowl of soup, its shape remains identical, and the same is true of ice, wood, and stone.

Juice, by contrast, is a liquid that flows, can be poured, and adopts the shape of whatever container holds it. Nevertheless, its volume does not change, so a cup of juice poured into a tall, narrow bottle is still precisely one cup of juice.

Air is a gas, and like most gases it is invisible. A gas will expand to fill any container entirely, regardless of how large or irregularly shaped that container may be, and it can also be squeezed into a smaller space, which is why a single tank can hold enough air to fill dozens of balloons.

The explanation for these differences involves particles, the microscopic pieces that make up all matter. In a solid, the particles are tightly packed and can only vibrate in fixed positions, while in a liquid they remain close to one another but are able to slide past each other. In a gas, the particles are widely separated and travel rapidly in every direction.

Heating supplies particles with additional energy, causing them to move faster and spread apart. When ice warms above zero degrees Celsius, it melts into liquid water, and when water reaches one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level, it boils and transforms into water vapor. Water also evaporates gradually at lower temperatures, which explains why puddles vanish on a sunny afternoon.

Cooling produces the opposite effect. On a humid day, droplets accumulate on a chilled can because water vapor in the surrounding air loses energy and changes back into liquid, a process called condensation. When liquid water becomes sufficiently cold, it freezes into solid ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, enormous facilities apply these transformations through a process called desalination, which removes salt from seawater. Some plants heat seawater until it becomes vapor, leaving the dissolved salt behind, and then cool the vapor so that it condenses into fresh water. Because the kingdom has very few rivers or lakes, desalination supplies much of the drinking water used in its cities.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around your kitchen and you might notice a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam drifting upward from a pot of rice. These objects appear entirely different from one another, yet they share a fundamental characteristic: each of them is composed of matter, which scientists define as anything that occupies space and possesses mass.

Most matter on Earth exists in one of three familiar forms, known as states: solid, liquid, and gas. Although an identical substance can exist in all three states, each state behaves in a distinctive and predictable way that scientists can explain.

A spoon is a solid, which means it has a definite shape and a definite volume, or quantity of space it occupies. Whether the spoon rests in a drawer or in a bowl of soup, its shape remains identical, and the same is true of ice, wood, and stone.

Juice, by contrast, is a liquid that flows, can be poured, and adopts the shape of whatever container holds it. Nevertheless, its volume remains constant, so a cup of juice transferred into a tall, narrow bottle is still precisely one cup of juice.

Air is a gas, and like most gases it is invisible. A gas will expand to fill any container entirely, regardless of how spacious or irregularly shaped that container may be, and it can also be compressed into a smaller space, which is why a single pressurized tank can contain enough air to inflate dozens of balloons.

The explanation for these differences involves particles, the microscopic units that make up all matter. In a solid, the particles are tightly packed and can only vibrate in fixed positions, whereas in a liquid they remain close to one another but are capable of sliding past each other. In a gas, the particles are widely separated and travel rapidly in every direction, colliding with one another and with the walls of their container.

Heating supplies particles with additional energy, causing them to move faster and separate further. When ice warms above zero degrees Celsius, it melts into liquid water, and when water reaches one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level, it boils and transforms into water vapor. Water also evaporates gradually at lower temperatures, which explains why puddles disappear on a sunny afternoon.

Cooling produces the opposite effect. On a humid day, droplets accumulate on a chilled can because water vapor in the surrounding atmosphere loses energy and reverts to liquid, a process called condensation, and when liquid water becomes sufficiently cold, it freezes into solid ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, enormous facilities apply these transformations through desalination, a process that removes salt from seawater. Certain plants heat seawater until it becomes vapor, leaving the dissolved minerals behind, and then cool the vapor so that it condenses into fresh water. Because the kingdom possesses very few permanent rivers or lakes, desalination provides a substantial proportion of the drinking water consumed in its cities.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look around your kitchen and you might observe a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam drifting upward from a pot of simmering rice. These objects appear entirely unrelated, yet they share a fundamental characteristic: each of them is composed of matter, which scientists define as anything that occupies space and possesses mass.

Most matter on Earth exists in one of three familiar forms, known as states, namely solid, liquid, and gas. Although an identical substance can exist in all three states, each state behaves in a distinctive and remarkably predictable manner that scientists can explain and measure.

A spoon is a solid, which means it possesses a definite shape and a definite volume, or quantity of space it occupies. Whether the spoon rests in a drawer or in a bowl of soup, its shape remains identical, and the same is true of ice, timber, and granite.

Juice, by contrast, is a liquid that flows, can be poured, and adopts the shape of whatever container holds it. Nevertheless, its volume remains constant, so a cup of juice transferred into a tall, narrow bottle is still precisely one cup of juice.

Air is a gas, and like most gases it is invisible. A gas will expand to fill any container entirely, regardless of how spacious or irregularly shaped that container may be, and it can also be compressed into a considerably smaller space, which is why a single pressurized cylinder can contain sufficient air to inflate dozens of balloons.

The explanation for these differences involves particles, the microscopic units that constitute all matter. In a solid, the particles are tightly packed and can only vibrate in fixed positions, whereas in a liquid they remain in close proximity but are capable of sliding past one another. In a gas, the particles are widely separated and travel rapidly in every direction, continually colliding with one another and with the walls of their container.

Heating supplies particles with additional energy, causing them to move more vigorously and separate further. When ice warms above zero degrees Celsius, it melts into liquid water, and when water reaches one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level, it boils and transforms into water vapor. Water also evaporates gradually at considerably lower temperatures, which explains why puddles disappear on a sunny afternoon.

Cooling produces the opposite effect. On a humid day, droplets accumulate on a chilled can because water vapor in the surrounding atmosphere loses energy and reverts to liquid, a process called condensation, and when liquid water becomes sufficiently cold, it solidifies into ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, enormous facilities apply these transformations through desalination, a process that removes dissolved salt from seawater. Certain plants heat seawater until it becomes vapor, leaving the concentrated minerals behind, and subsequently cool the vapor so that it condenses into fresh water. Because the kingdom possesses very few permanent rivers or lakes, desalination provides a substantial proportion of the drinking water consumed in its rapidly expanding cities.

versions.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
versions.text:
Look attentively around your kitchen and you might observe a metal spoon, a glass of orange juice, and steam drifting upward from a pot of simmering rice. These objects appear entirely unrelated, yet they share a fundamental characteristic, because each of them is composed of matter, which scientists define as anything that occupies space and possesses mass.

Most matter on Earth exists in one of three familiar forms, known as states, namely solid, liquid, and gas. Although an identical substance can exist in all three states, each state behaves in a distinctive and remarkably predictable manner that scientists can explain, measure, and apply in practical technologies.

A spoon is a solid, which means it possesses a definite shape and a definite volume, or quantity of space it occupies. Whether the spoon rests in a drawer or in a bowl of soup, its shape remains identical, and the same principle applies to ice, timber, granite, and countless other substances.

Juice, by contrast, is a liquid that flows, can be poured, and adopts the shape of whatever container holds it, although its volume remains constant, so a cup of juice transferred into a tall, narrow bottle is still precisely one cup of juice, however different it may appear.

Air is an invisible gas, and like every gas it will expand to occupy any container entirely, regardless of how spacious or irregularly shaped that container may be, and it can additionally be compressed into a considerably smaller space, which explains why a single pressurized cylinder can contain sufficient air to inflate dozens of balloons.

The explanation for these differences involves particles, the microscopic units that constitute all matter. In a solid, the particles are tightly packed and can only vibrate in fixed positions, whereas in a liquid they remain in close proximity but are capable of sliding past one another. In a gas, the particles are widely separated and travel rapidly in every direction, continually colliding with one another and with the boundaries of their container.

Heating supplies particles with additional energy, causing them to move more vigorously and separate further. When ice warms above zero degrees Celsius, it melts into liquid water, and when water reaches one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level, it boils and transforms into water vapor. Water also evaporates gradually at considerably lower temperatures, which explains why puddles disappear on a sunny afternoon even though the water never boils.

Cooling produces the opposite effect. On a humid afternoon, droplets accumulate on a chilled can because water vapor in the surrounding atmosphere loses energy and reverts to liquid, a process called condensation, and when liquid water becomes sufficiently cold, it solidifies into ice.

Along the coasts of Saudi Arabia, enormous facilities apply these transformations through desalination, a technological process that removes dissolved salt from seawater. Certain plants heat seawater until it becomes vapor, leaving the concentrated minerals behind, and subsequently cool the vapor so that it condenses into fresh water. Because the kingdom possesses very few permanent rivers or lakes, desalination provides a substantial proportion of the drinking water consumed in its rapidly expanding urban communities.

keyWords.definition: all the stuff that things are made of
keyWords.example: A chair, a drop of rain, and the air in a ball are all matter.

keyWords.definition: something that keeps its own shape, like a rock or a book
keyWords.example: A brick is a solid, so it stays the same shape in your hand.

keyWords.definition: something wet that can flow and be poured, like water
keyWords.example: Laban is a liquid that my mother pours into small cups.

keyWords.definition: something like air that spreads out to fill a space
keyWords.example: The gas inside the balloon made it big and round.

keyWords.definition: to change from a solid into a liquid because of heat
keyWords.example: Chocolate will melt if you leave it in a hot car.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to make ice in a freezer
The three forms of matter and how they change
Why rocks are harder than wood
How to drink more water on hot days
questions.why: The article tells about solids, liquids, and gases and how heat and cold change them.

wrong.A: Ice is one example, but the article is not about using a freezer.
wrong.C: The article does not compare how hard rocks and wood are.
wrong.D: The article does not give tips about drinking water.

questions.stem: What does a liquid do when you pour it into a cup?
options: It keeps its own shape.
It turns into a gas.
It takes the shape of the cup.
It gets hard like a rock.
questions.why: The article says a liquid flows and takes the shape of the cup it is in.

wrong.A: A solid keeps its own shape, not a liquid.
wrong.B: Pouring does not turn a liquid into a gas. Heat does that.
wrong.D: Getting hard is what happens when water freezes, not when it is poured.

questions.stem: Which thing does the article name as a gas?
options: Air
Ice
Milk
A rock
questions.why: The article says air is a gas that spreads out to fill space.

wrong.D: A rock is a solid.

questions.stem: The article says heat makes ice melt. What does melt mean?
options: To get colder and harder
To break into small pieces
To float to the top of water
To change from a solid to a liquid
questions.why: When ice melts, the solid ice turns into liquid water.

wrong.A: Getting colder and harder is freezing, the opposite of melting.
wrong.B: Breaking into pieces does not change ice into water.
wrong.C: The article does not talk about ice floating.

questions.stem: What makes drops of water form on a cold can on a hot day?
options: The can has a hole in it.
Gas in the air cools and turns into water.
The sun makes the can sweat.
Ice inside the can melts through the metal.
questions.why: The article explains that the gas in the air cools on the can and turns back into water.

wrong.A: The article does not say the can has a hole.
wrong.C: Cans do not sweat; the water comes from the air.
wrong.D: Water cannot pass through the metal of the can.

questions.stem: A boy leaves a glass of water in a very cold freezer all night. What will most likely happen?
options: The water will turn into ice.
The water will turn into a gas.
The water will spread out to fill the freezer.
The water will stay the same.
questions.why: The article says very cold water turns into ice, a solid.

wrong.B: Water turns into a gas when it is heated, not cooled.
wrong.C: Only a gas spreads out to fill all the space.
wrong.D: The article shows that cold changes water.

questions.stem: Why do the big plants by the sea heat sea water?
options: To make the sea warmer for swimming
To make more salt for cooking
To get fresh water without salt
To turn the water into ice
questions.why: When the water turns into a gas, the salt stays behind, and the gas cools into fresh water to drink.

wrong.A: The plants heat water inside the plant, not the sea for swimmers.
wrong.B: The salt is left behind, but the goal is fresh water.
wrong.D: Heating turns water into a gas, not ice.

questions.stem: How does the author explain each form of matter?
options: By telling a story about one family
By giving an example for each form, like a rock, milk, and air
By listing the forms from oldest to newest
By asking the reader many questions with no answers
questions.why: The author uses an example for each form: a rock for solid, a drink for liquid, and air for gas.

wrong.A: The article is not a story about a family.
wrong.C: The forms of matter are not old or new.
wrong.D: The article gives facts, not questions without answers.

LOW.prompt: Pick one thing in your home that is a solid, one that is a liquid, and one that is a gas. Tell how you know which form each one is, using facts from the article.
checklist: I named one solid, one liquid, and one gas.
I used facts from the article to explain each one.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: In my home, a metal spoon is a solid because it keeps its own shape no matter where I put it. A glass of juice is a liquid, because it flows and takes the shape of its cup, but the amount stays the same. The steam rising from a hot pot is a gas, because it spreads out and fills the air around it. All three are forms of matter, and if I heated the spoon enough, it would even melt into a liquid.

keyWords.definition: a very tiny piece of something
keyWords.example: A particle of dust floated in the sunlight by the window.

keyWords.definition: to shake quickly back and forth in a small space
keyWords.example: My phone began to vibrate on the table when my aunt called.

keyWords.definition: something that holds things inside it, like a box, jar, or bottle
keyWords.example: Grandmother keeps the dates in a plastic container.

keyWords.definition: to change slowly from a liquid into a gas
keyWords.example: Water in the bird bath will evaporate by the end of a hot day.

keyWords.definition: the change of a gas into a liquid when it cools
keyWords.example: Condensation made the bathroom mirror foggy after my shower.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Water is the only kind of matter that can change.
Matter comes in three states that behave differently and can change with heating or cooling.
Gases are more useful than solids and liquids.
Saudi Arabia has more water than any other country.
questions.why: The article explains solids, liquids, and gases, why they act differently, and how heat and cold change them.

wrong.A: Water is the main example, but the article does not say it is the only matter that changes.
wrong.C: The article does not rank the states as more or less useful.
wrong.D: The article says the kingdom makes drinking water from seawater, not that it has the most water.

questions.stem: How do the particles in a liquid move?
options: They stay close but slide past one another.
They stay in one place and only vibrate.
They are far apart and move quickly in every direction.
They do not move at all.
questions.why: The article says liquid particles remain close but can slide past one another.

wrong.B: Only vibrating in place describes a solid.
wrong.C: Being far apart and moving fast describes a gas.
wrong.D: The article says particles in every state move in some way.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens to a gas in a container?
options: It sinks to the bottom.
It keeps its own shape.
It fills the container completely.
It turns into a liquid right away.
questions.why: The article says a gas spreads out to fill any container completely.

wrong.A: Sinking to the bottom is what a liquid does, not a gas.
wrong.B: A solid keeps its own shape.
wrong.D: A gas only turns into a liquid when it cools.

questions.stem: In a solid, particles can only vibrate in place. What does vibrate mean here?
options: Grow bigger and bigger
Shake back and forth in a small space
Float slowly upward
Join together into one piece
questions.why: Particles in a solid are packed tightly, so they can only shake a little without moving away.

wrong.C: The particles stay in place; they do not float away.
wrong.D: The particles stay separate pieces even when packed tightly.

questions.stem: Why do particles move faster when matter is heated?

MID.prompt: Explain what happens to the particles of water as ice melts and then boils. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I described the particles in the solid, liquid, and gas.
I used at least two details from the article.
I put the changes in the correct order.
MID.modelAnswer: As ice melts and then boils, the particles of water change a lot. In solid ice, the particles are packed close together and can only vibrate in place, which is why ice holds a solid shape. When the ice warms up and melts, the particles gain enough energy to slide past each other, and the water becomes a liquid that can evaporate slowly or take the shape of its container. If the liquid water is heated even more, it boils, and the particles spread far apart and move quickly as a gas called water vapor, while condensation happens later if that vapor cools back down.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how desalination uses two changes of state to turn seawater into drinking water. Support your explanation with evidence from the article.
checklist: I named both changes of state and put them in order.
I supported my explanation with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained why the salt is left behind.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Desalination turns seawater into drinking water by using two changes of state in a careful order. First, large plants heat the salty seawater until its particles gain enough energy to expand apart and evaporate into water vapor, and because salt does not turn into a gas the way water does, the salt is left behind. Second, the rising vapor is then cooled until condensation occurs, changing the particles back into a liquid, but this time the liquid is pure, fresh water with none of the original salt's volume mixed in. By evaporating the water away from the salt and then condensing it separately, these plants along the coasts of Saudi Arabia can produce the fresh water that the region's climate alone cannot reliably provide.
